content: The endometrium is the innermost lining of the uterus in mammals. Its primary function is to serve as a protective lining for the uterus, preventing the walls of the myometrium from adhering to one another and maintaining the openness of the uterine cavity. During the menstrual or estrous cycle, the endometrium thickens and becomes enriched with blood vessels and glandular tissue. This thickened layer provides an ideal environment for the implantation of a blastocyst when it reaches the uterus. If pregnancy occurs, the glands and blood vessels within the endometrium further expand in size and number. The vascular spaces merge and interconnect, forming the placenta, which is responsible for delivering oxygen and nutrients to the developing embryo and fetus. The endometrial lining undergoes cyclic regeneration. In humans and great apes, this process is part of the menstrual cycle, while in most other mammals, it is part of the estrous cycle. Initially, the endometrium proliferates under the influence of estrogen. After ovulation, the ovary begins producing progesterone in addition to estrogen. This hormonal shift transforms the endometrium from a proliferative state to a secretory lining, which creates a supportive environment for potential blastocyst implantation. If no blastocyst is detected, progesterone levels drop, and the endometrial lining is either reabsorbed (in the estrous cycle) or shed (in the menstrual cycle). In the case of menstruation, the shedding process involves the breakdown of the endometrial lining, rupture of small blood vessels, and expulsion of tissue and blood through the vagina over several days. Uterine contractions often accompany this process to aid in expelling the menstrual endometrium. If implantation occurs, the endometrial lining is not shed or reabsorbed. Instead, it transforms into the decidua, which becomes part of the placenta and provides structural support and protection for the pregnancy. Inadequate hormonal stimulation, particularly a lack of estrogen or progesterone, can result in a thin, inactive endometrium. In humans, this condition leads to amenorrhea (absence of menstruation). After menopause, the endometrial lining typically becomes atrophic. Conversely, chronic exposure to estrogen without progesterone can cause the endometrium to become hyperplastic. In humans, the cycle of building and shedding the endometrial lining averages 28 days. The rate of endometrial development varies among mammals and can be influenced by factors such as seasons, climate, stress, and other conditions. The endometrium itself produces certain hormones at different points in the cycle, which can affect other parts of the reproductive system. Histologically, the endometrium consists of a single layer of columnar epithelium resting on a connective tissue layer called the stroma, which varies in thickness depending on hormonal influences. Simple tubular uterine glands extend from the endometrial surface to the base of the stroma, which is richly supplied with spiral arteries. In women of reproductive age, the endometrium has two distinct layers: the functional layer and the basal layer. The functional layer is adjacent to the uterine cavity and regenerates after menstruation during the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle under the influence of estrogen. It further thickens during the luteal phase due to progesterone from the corpus luteum, creating an optimal environment for embryo implantation and growth. This layer is completely shed during menstruation. The basal layer lies beneath the functional layer, adjacent to the myometrium. It is not shed during the menstrual cycle and serves as the source for regenerating the functional layer. In the absence of progesterone, the arteries supplying the functional layer constrict, leading to ischemia and cell death, which results in menstruation. The phase of the menstrual cycle can be identified by observing histological differences in the endometrium. Pathological conditions of the endometrium include adenomyosis, where endometrial tissue grows into the myometrium, and endometriosis, where endometrial tissue grows outside the uterus. Endometrial cancer is the most common malignancy of the female genital tract.
